title: I stake, use DeFi or have received airdrops
excerpt: How transactions that aren't a simple purchase and sale are taxed: staking rewards, liquidity pools, lending, yield farming and tokens received without buying them.

hero.h1: Your activity doesn't fit into “I bought and I sold”
hero.subheading: You deposited into a pool, received a token representing your position, collected rewards, lent, borrowed. None of those things is a purchase or a sale, and each one has its own treatment.

sections.body:
Crypto asset taxation is almost always explained with the simplest example: you buy bitcoin, sell it for more and pay tax on the difference. Your activity looks nothing like that.

In DeFi there are intermediate steps with no obvious equivalent in the traditional world. You deposit two assets into a pool and receive a token representing your share: is that a swap? You withdraw and get back different amounts from the ones you put in: where is the gain? You collect rewards in a token that isn't listed anywhere well known: at what value do you declare them?

Not all of those questions have a clear, published answer from the tax authorities, and that is where the real work lies: applying a defensible approach, documenting it and staying consistent with it across every tax year. A reasonable, consistent approach is worth far more than an aggressive one.

sections.entrada: Almost all DeFi activity ends up in one of these two boxes, and they are neither taxed nor offset in the same way.

items: Selling a crypto asset for euros
Swapping one token for another, including entering and exiting many pools
Disposing of a token that represents a position
It goes into the savings tax base and follows its offsetting rules
Rewards for making your crypto assets available to a third party
Taxed when received, not when sold
Different rules apply: it isn't offset in the same way as a capital loss

bullets: Staking: rewards are taxed when you receive them, at their value on that date. That value becomes the acquisition cost of the tokens received, which stops you being taxed twice on the same thing when you sell them.

Liquidity pools: the critical point is how entering and exiting the pool is treated, along with the token that represents the position. This is where approaches diverge most, and where documenting the one applied is essential.
Yield farming: layers of rewards on top of already complex positions, often in tokens without a deep market. The difficulty isn't the approach, it's the valuation.
Lending and borrowing: interest earned and interest paid are not treated symmetrically, and collateral liquidations have effects of their own.
Airdrops: the key is fixing the value on the date of receipt, because that will be your acquisition cost. And telling a genuine airdrop apart from spam tokens you never asked for.

Bridging and wrapping: moving an asset between chains or wrapping it doesn't always get the same treatment as a swap, and treating it wrongly multiplies phantom transactions across the whole portfolio.

steps.title: We reconstruct your on-chain activity
steps.body: An exchange's CSV isn't enough: most of this happens on-chain and has to be read from there, protocol by protocol.

steps.title: We identify how each protocol really works
steps.body: Before deciding the tax treatment, you have to understand what happened technically. Two protocols that look the same can work differently under the hood.

steps.title: We set an approach and document it
steps.body: Where there is no clear position from the tax authorities, a reasonable one is applied, the reasons are written down and it is kept consistent across every tax year. Consistency can be defended; improvisation can't.

steps.title: We value what has no obvious price
steps.body: For tokens without a deep market, the price source and the date are documented. It's the first thing to be questioned if it is ever reviewed.

steps.title: We integrate it with the rest of your portfolio
steps.body: Because the offsetting rules link everything together, and a decision in DeFi affects the overall result.

items.q: Am I taxed on rewards even if I haven't sold them?
items.a: Income from making your crypto assets available to others is taxed when it is received, not when it is converted into euros. The flip side is that the value taxed becomes your acquisition cost, so when you sell you are only taxed on any later difference.

items.q: My rewards are in a token that's worth almost nothing
items.a: They are still taxed, at their value on the date you receive them, however small. What needs care is the price source and how it is documented, because for tokens without a deep market, prices vary widely between sources.

items.q: I entered and exited a pool with different amounts
items.a: That's normal, and it's where the work lies. You have to reconstruct what was contributed, what the position token represented and what was recovered, and apply a consistent approach to both entry and exit. It's one of the situations that always ends up in manual review.

items.q: What about the spam tokens that appear in my wallet?
items.a: Turning up at your address doesn't make something your airdrop. Spam is filtered with judgement, not with an automatic list, and the filter applied is documented. On chains such as Solana there can be thousands of records which, if processed as income, throw off the entire portfolio.

Most of them. The difficult cases are very small protocols, ones with no maintained explorer or ones that no longer exist. If your activity includes any of those, we tell you before we start rather than finding out halfway through.

cierre.h2: Tell us which protocols you've used
cierre.body: Once we know which chains you operate on, which protocols you have used and since when, we can tell you which parts can be reconstructed, where an approach will need to be set and what work lies ahead.
